There is one joy of childhood, however, which one can never recapture, and that is the joy of getting wet in the sea. There is a statue not so far from Fleet Street of the man who introduced Sunday schools into England, but the man whom boys and girls would really like to commemorate in lasting stone is the doctor who first said that salt water couldn't give you a cold. Whether this was true or not I do not know, but it was a splendid and never-failing retort to anxious grown-ups, and added much to the joys of the seaside. But it is a joy no longer possible to one who is his own master. I, for instance, can get my feet wet in fresh water if I like; to get them wet in salt water is no special privilege.

Feeling as I do, writing as I have written, it is sad for me to know that if I really went to the sea this August it would not be with a spade and a bucket but with a bag of golf clubs; that even my evenings would be spent, not on the beach, but on a bicycle riding to the nearest town for a paper. Yet it is useless for you to say that I do not love the sea with my old love, that I am no longer pleased with the old childish things. I shall maintain that it is the sea which is not what it was, and that I am very happy in Fleet Street thinking of it as it used to be.

message.content:
One aspect of childhood that remains forever elusive is the sheer delight of splashing in the ocean. Near Fleet Street, there's a statue honoring the individual who pioneered Sunday schools in England. However, the true hero deserving of a permanent tribute in stone is the physician who asserted that saltwater could not cause colds. I cannot attest to the accuracy of that claim, but it served as an excellent and unwavering comeback to concerned adults, enhancing the pleasure of seaside experiences. Sadly, that thrill is no longer accessible to those who have grown up. For example, while I can choose to soak my feet in freshwater whenever I wish, wading into saltwater no longer feels like a unique privilege.

Considering my current sentiments and the reflections expressed in my writing, it is disheartening to acknowledge that a trip to the sea this August would not involve a spade and bucket, but rather a set of golf clubs. My evenings would not be spent basking on the sand, but rather pedaling my bicycle to the nearest town to pick up a newspaper. Yet, it would be misguided to suggest that my affection for the sea has waned or that I no longer find joy in the simple pleasures of my youth. I firmly believe that it is the essence of the sea itself that has changed, and I find solace in reminiscing about its former magic while I remain in Fleet Street, cherishing the memories of what it once was.
